analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal antitrust exemption for the insurance industry.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee: introduced with no cosponsors, it received no hearing or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has shielded the insurance business from most federal antitrust rules, letting insurers coordinate on prices and practices in ways other industries cannot. This bill would erase that shield, subjecting insurance companies to the same competition laws as everyone else. The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance customers, and businesses that buy insurance. Repealing the exemption would mean insurers could no longer rely on federal antitrust immunity to coordinate on rates or market practices, and could face antitrust suits for practices like price fixing — a change economists and consumer groups have argued could pressure premiums down through more competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People and businesses who buy insurance

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the McCarran-Ferguson Act, the 1945 law that exempts the 'business of insurance' from federal antitrust laws [S2] [S3].
With the exemption gone, insurance companies would be subject to the same federal antitrust rules as other businesses [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The insurance industry, which would lose its special immunity from antitrust laws and could face antitrust enforcement over rate-setting and joint activities it currently performs under the exemption.

drawbacks.text: State insurance regulators and the industry have long argued the exemption allows small insurers to pool claims data and share risk information, which they say keeps coverage available in high-risk markets; removing it could expose legitimate data-sharing to legal challenge and raise costs for some policyholders. This concern is not addressed in the bill or its summary [S2] [S3].
The bill offered no transition or carve-outs; it repealed the entire 1945 act in one sentence [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A full repeal would put insurers under the same competition rules as everyone else, which most directly benefits policyholders. The genuine tradeoff is that some cooperative activities insurers say benefit consumers, like pooling loss data, would sit in a legal gray zone, and the bill offered no carve-out to address that. Its lack of any cosponsors suggests even its potential supporters saw the one-sentence approach as too blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Garn introduced the bill on August 2, 1991 [S1] [S2].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill had no cosponsors [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies, which kept their federal antitrust exemption because the bill never advanced; state regulators' oversight arrangement also stayed untouched.

for.name: Sen. E. J. (Jake) Garn
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the McCarran-Ferguson Act.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced it and found no cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no partisan split — only a lack of any visible support.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped insurers' federal antitrust exemption, exposing rate coordination and joint market practices to antitrust law. Insurance is something nearly every household and business must buy, so less coordination and more competition generally runs in policyholders' favor.

McCarran-Ferguson also anchors state regulation of insurance; a full repeal without a replacement framework could have disrupted how states oversee insurers. Regulators were not a named actor in the record, but repeal of their statutory footing is a real effect of the bill's text.
